title: Respectful communication and coordinated support
audience: Coordinators, support workers and trained cleaners who may be asked to work in a home affected by hoarding or environmental neglect, as part of an authorised support plan. Not a qualification or authority to clear a property, dispose of a resident's belongings, enter by force, or provide welfare or clinical support.
learningOutcomes: Use neutral, person-centred language in a role-play about the work.
Agree communication roles, privacy rules and an escalation contact with the resident.
Stop and report a privacy breach, and record it through the incident procedure.

instruction.heading: Scope of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson covers communication, privacy and coordination. It does not give welfare, clinical or safeguarding assessments, and completing it does not qualify a worker to make them. Those decisions belong to the people responsible for them under the support plan.

instruction.heading: Language and dignity
instruction.body: Describe the situation in neutral, factual words. Clutter and environmental neglect are not personal failings. The Victorian Department of Families, Fairness and Housing describes hoarding as keeping many things that others think are useless or have little or no value, and notes that hoarding is different from collecting, where collectors are usually well organised and collect one type of thing. Avoid words that shame the person, and avoid photographs that expose the home to others. Speak to the resident about what they want to achieve, not about what others think should go.

instruction.heading: Coordinated support and privacy
instruction.body: Agree communication roles, break times, privacy rules and one escalation contact with the resident before the first session. Invite only the supporters the resident has authorised. The DFFH page refers to Make Safe guidance written for services such as councils, healthcare providers and housing providers, and that guidance should be used through the coordinator rather than applied alone. The CFA says hoarding is a complex issue which requires intervention and long-term support, so a cleaning crew should not be the only service involved. A worker who shares a before-photograph of the home in a group chat has breached the resident's privacy. Stop sharing, tell the coordinator, follow the incident procedure and keep the information confidential.

procedure: Agree communication roles, break times, privacy rules and the escalation contact with the resident.
Confirm who the resident has authorised to take part, and record it.
Use neutral, factual language, and avoid words that shame.
Take no photographs beyond the authorised record, and share none.
If a supporter asks for information the resident has not authorised, decline and refer it to the coordinator.
Record each agreement and any breach, and report the breach through the incident procedure.

workedExamples.situation: A crew member shares a before-photograph of a resident's home in a family group chat.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop sharing, tell the coordinator, follow the privacy and incident procedure and keep the information confidential. The group chat is not an authorised audience.

workedExamples.situation: The resident says the family wants a daily update with photographs of every room.
workedExamples.reasoning: Check the resident's authorisation for each recipient and for each photograph. Share only what the resident has agreed to share, and refer the rest to the coordinator.

equipmentAndPpe: Written communication plan with roles, break times, privacy rules and the escalation contact.
Authorisation list of the people the resident has approved to take part.
Role-play scripts. No real residents, homes or images are used in this lesson.

commonErrors.error: Using words such as 'filthy' or 'disgusting' with the resident or family.
commonErrors.prevention: Use neutral, factual words and describe the work, not the person.

commonErrors.error: Sharing images of the home with people who are not authorised.
commonErrors.prevention: Limit records and sharing to what the resident has authorised, and confirm recipients in advance.

commonErrors.error: Telling the resident the job is about making the home look acceptable to others.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the agreed safety objective in the resident's own terms.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Privacy and the disclosure of health, drug use or personal circumstances are governed by privacy law and by the authority that holds the record. This lesson does not set out those rules.
Completing this lesson does not qualify a worker to provide welfare, clinical or safeguarding assessments.

qualityStandard: The learner uses neutral, person-centred language in a role-play.
The learner identifies who is authorised to receive information and photographs.
The learner stops a breach, reports it and records the incident.
documentationEvidence: Communication plan with roles, break times, privacy rules and the escalation contact.
Record of who the resident has authorised to take part.
Incident record for any breach, with the actions taken.
summary: Describe the situation, not the person.
Agree roles, privacy rules and an escalation contact before work starts.
Share nothing the resident has not authorised.
A breach is stopped, reported and recorded.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which opening statement is most respectful for a first conversation about the work?
options: 'We agreed to make the route to your bathroom safe. Shall we go through what you would like kept?'
'This place is a health hazard and must be cleaned today.'
'Your family says it is out of hand, so we will sort it out.'

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker sends a before-photograph of a home to a family group chat. What is the correct response?
options: Delete the photograph from the chat and carry on.
Stop sharing, tell the coordinator and follow the privacy and incident procedure.
Ask the family to keep it private and continue.

knowledgeChecks.question: A relative asks for photographs of every room each day. What should happen?
options: Send them, because the relative is supportive.
Send them to the coordinator only, without asking the resident.
Check the resident's authorisation for the recipient and the photographs, share only what is authorised, and refer the rest to the coordinator.

officialReferences.title: Hoarding and environmental neglect (Department of Families, Fairness and Housing, Victoria, provider page)
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool on 2026-11-03. The page defines hoarding as keeping many things that others think are useless or have little or no value; says hoarding is different from collecting, where collectors are usually well organised and collect one type of thing; and cites the Make Safe guidance for services working with people living with hoarding and environmental neglect. Publisher: Department of Families, Fairness and Housing (Victoria).

officialReferences.title: Hoarding and fire safety (Country Fire Authority, Victoria)
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool on 2026-11-03. The page says clutter can easily catch fire and increase the intensity of a fire; hoarding makes fires more likely to start; hallways, windows and doors can become blocked, so getting in and out is harder; hoarded objects can stop sprinkler water reaching a fire in apartments; one-off clean-ups do not deal with the underlying reasons for hoarding behaviour; and hoarding is a complex issue requiring intervention and long-term support. Publisher: Country Fire Authority (Victoria).

moduleAuthority.heading: Module authority and restricted work
moduleAuthority.body: This module is training content. It does not grant authority to enter a home by force, to clear, sort or dispose of a resident's belongings without valid consent, to handle or dispose of hazardous waste, to deal with unstable stacks or structural hazards, or to provide welfare, clinical or safeguarding assessments. Completing this lesson does not give a licence, certificate or approval. Work is done only under an authorised support plan and a written agreement with the resident, within the limits set by the employer and the local law. Tenancy, safeguarding and information-sharing rights are jurisdiction-specific, and fire-risk, structural, pest and hazardous-waste decisions belong to the competent authorities and specialists named in the plan. Where authority or consent is unclear, stop and refer.

stopWorkAndReferral.heading: Stop-work and referral rules for this module
stopWorkAndReferral.body: Stop and refer whenever any of these is true: consent is not specific, documented and current; the resident has objected or withdrawn consent; a party seeks entry by force, nonconsensual disposal or removal of personal documents; a fire-load, ignition, egress or obstruction hazard is present; a stack or structure is unstable; pests, unknown liquids or mouldy goods are present; sharps, chemicals or unknown containers are found; waste would go to general disposal without characterisation; private information is requested without authority; or the work would go beyond the approved plan. Stopping is a valid professional outcome. Record the disagreement, protect the resident's choices and refer the authority dispute before any property is moved.
